questions.problem: Calculate $\int 4\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡2x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Rearranging the above formula, we get

$$
2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x=4\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int 2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)+C \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area $A$ of the region in the $xy$-plane that is bounded by the curve $y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2}),$ the $x$-axis and the lines $x=\frac{\pi }{6}$ and $x=\frac{5\pi }{6},$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the region is given by

$$
A={\int }_{\pi /6}^{5\pi /6}4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\,\text{d}x.
$$

In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta 
$$

Letting $\theta =\frac{x}{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{5\pi /6}4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{5\pi /6}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,{|}_{\pi /6}^{5\pi /6} \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6})+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: $\int \operatorname{sin}⁡3x\operatorname{cos}⁡3x\,\text{d}x=$
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,⇒\,\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

 

Letting $\theta =3x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡6x & =\operatorname{sin}⁡3x\operatorname{cos}⁡3x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡3x\operatorname{cos}⁡3x\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡6x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{cos}⁡6x)+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{cos}⁡6x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: ${\int }_{0}^{\pi /10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5x}{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5x}{2})\text{d}x=$
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,⇒\,\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

 

Letting $\theta =\frac{5x}{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡5x & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5x}{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5x}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5x}{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5x}{2})\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /10}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡5x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /10}\operatorname{sin}⁡5x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡5x]}_{0}^{\pi /10} \\  & =-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{cos}⁡5x\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /10} \\  & =-\frac{1}{10}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\cdot \frac{\pi }{10})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\cdot 0)] \\  & =-\frac{1}{10}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)] \\  & =-\frac{1}{10}\cdot [0-1] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area $A$ of the region in the $xy$-plane that is bounded by the curve $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{6})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{6}),$ the $x$-axis and the lines $x=0$ and $x=\frac{3\pi }{2},$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the region is given by

$$
A={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{6})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{6})\,\text{d}x.
$$

In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta 
$$

Letting $\theta =\frac{x}{6},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{3}) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{6})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{6}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{6})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{6})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{3})\,{|}_{0}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+3\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta 
$$

Letting $\theta =\frac{x}{3},$ we get

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2x}{3})={cos}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{3})-{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{3}).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-3\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}\frac{1}{2}({cos}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{3})-{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{3}))\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-3\pi /4}^{3\pi /4}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2x}{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2x}{3})\,{|}_{-3\pi /4}^{3\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{3\pi }{4})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2}{3}\cdot (-\frac{3\pi }{4}))] \\  & =\frac{3}{4}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =\frac{3}{4}(1-(-1)) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: $\int ({cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x)\text{d}x=$
questions.worked_solution:
We can use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta 
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x)\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area $A$ of the region in the $xy$-plane that is bounded by the curve $y=6{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)-6{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+3x+17,$ the $x$-axis and the lines $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $x=0,$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the region is given by

$$
A={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}(6{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)-6{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+3x+17)\,\text{d}x.
$$

To calculate this integral, we use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x={cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x
$$

We can rewrite the above formula as

$$
6\operatorname{cos}⁡4x=6{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)-6{sin}^{2}⁡(2x).
$$

Hence, the area of the region is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}(6{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)-6{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)+3x+17)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+3x+17)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+17x)\,{|}_{-\pi /2}^{0} \\  & =[\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+\frac{3}{2}(0)^{2}+17\cdot 0]-[\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-2\pi )+\frac{3}{2}{(-\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}+17(-\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =[0+0+0]-[0+\frac{3{\pi }^{2}}{8}-\frac{17\pi }{2}] \\  & =[0+\frac{17\pi }{2}-\frac{3{\pi }^{2}}{8}]-0 \\  & =\frac{17\pi }{2}-\frac{3{\pi }^{2}}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}({sin}^{2}⁡4x-{cos}^{2}⁡4x)\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

Letting $\theta =4x,$ we get

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡8x={cos}^{2}⁡4x-{sin}^{2}⁡4x.
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}({sin}^{2}⁡4x-{cos}^{2}⁡4x)\text{d}x & =-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}({cos}^{2}⁡4x-{sin}^{2}⁡4x)\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡8x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡8x\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(8\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(8\cdot 0)] \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}[\operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0] \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}(0-0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the region is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}A={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+2-x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate this integral, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡x$ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=2{cos}^{2}⁡x-1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2{cos}^{2}⁡(2x)+2-x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[(\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+1)+2-x]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+3-x)\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+3x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =[\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )+3\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{1}{2}{(\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}]-[\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+3(0)-\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2}] \\  & =[\frac{3\pi }{2}-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8}]-[0] \\  & =\frac{12\pi -{\pi }^{2}}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate $\int 4{cos}^{4}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta =\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +1.
$$

Taking $\theta =x$ and substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4{cos}^{4}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int {(2{cos}^{2}⁡x)}^{2}\text{d}x \\  & =\int {(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1)}^{2}\text{d}x \\  & =\int ({cos}^{2}⁡2x+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1)\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the same formula $2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta =\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +1$ with $\theta =2x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({cos}^{2}⁡2x+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1)\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+1)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\frac{3}{2})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x)+2(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+\frac{3}{2}\,x+C \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+\frac{3x}{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Recall  ${cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x=1,$ so we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}5{sin}^{2}⁡x+11{cos}^{2}⁡x & =5{sin}^{2}⁡x+5{cos}^{2}⁡x+6{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =5({sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x)+6{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =5+6{cos}^{2}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡x$ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=2{cos}^{2}⁡x-1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(5+6{cos}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[5+6\cdot \frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1)]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(8+3\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)\text{d}x \\  & ={(8x+\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =[8\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})]-[8(0)+\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(0))] \\  & =[4\pi +\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )]-[0+\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)] \\  & =[4\pi +\frac{3}{2}(0)]-[0+\frac{3}{2}(0)] \\  & =4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

$$
A={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi /2}(3{cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x & =2{cos}^{2}⁡x+({sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x) \\  & =2{cos}^{2}⁡x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡x$ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=2{cos}^{2}⁡x-1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
2{cos}^{2}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1.
$$

Hence, the area of the region is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi /2}(2{cos}^{2}⁡x+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+2x)\,|}_{-\pi }^{\pi /2} \\  & =(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})+2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})-(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot (-\pi ))+2(-\pi )) \\  & =(0+\pi )-(0-2\pi ) \\  & =\pi +2\pi  \\  & =3\pi .\end{aligned}

questions.worked_solution:
The area of the region bounded by the curve $y={x}^{2}-{sin}^{2}⁡x,$ the $x$-axis and the lines $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $x=\pi $ is

$$
A={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }({x}^{2}-{sin}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${sin}^{2}$ term: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=1-2{sin}^{2}⁡x
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-1)=-{sin}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Hence, the area of the region is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }({x}^{2}-{sin}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-1))\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-\frac{1}{2}x)|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =(\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{3}+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{\pi }{2})-(\frac{(\pi /2)^{3}}{3}+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =(\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{3}-\frac{\pi }{2})-(\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{24}-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{7{\pi }^{3}}{24}-\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14039635/assets/07a1fab6073fdff2a20140719b570c0c40981ab049866480fbaff4dfad0c7799.png)

Find the area $A$ of the region in the $xy$-plane that is bounded by the curve $y=\frac{7}{2}{sin}^{2}⁡(2x),$ the $x$-axis, and the lines $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ and $x=\frac{5\pi }{4}$, as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the region bounded by the curve $y=\frac{7}{2}{sin}^{2}⁡(2x),$ the $x$-axis and the lines $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ and $x=\frac{5\pi }{4}$ is 

$$
A={\int }_{\pi /4}^{5\pi /4}\frac{7}{2}{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${sin}^{2}$ term: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

Letting $\theta =2x,$ we have

$$
\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x))={sin}^{2}⁡(2x).
$$

We can now integrate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{5\pi /4}\frac{7}{2}{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{7}{2}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{5\pi /4}\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x))\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{7}{4}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{5\pi /4}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x))\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{7}{4}{(x-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x))|}_{\pi /4}^{5\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{7}{4}[(\frac{5\pi }{4}-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\pi ))-(\frac{\pi }{4}-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ))] \\  & =\frac{7}{4}(\frac{5\pi }{4}-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${sin}^{2}$ term: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=1-2{sin}^{2}⁡x.
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=2{sin}^{2}⁡x.
$$

We can now integrate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (4{sin}^{2}⁡x+6x)\text{d}x & =\int (2\cdot 2{sin}^{2}⁡x+6x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)+6x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+6x)\text{d}x \\  & =2x-2(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+6(\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+C \\  & =2x-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+3{x}^{2}+C \\  & =3{x}^{2}+2x-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+C\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\sin {2\theta} =2\sin \theta \cos \theta\quad\Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{1}{2}\sin(2\theta) = \sin{\theta}\cos{\theta}.
$$

 

Letting $\theta= \dfrac{x}{2},$ we get

$$
\eqalign{
\dfrac{1}{2} \sin \left(2\cdot \dfrac{x}{2} \right) &= \sin \left(\dfrac{x}{2} \right)\cos\left( \dfrac{x}{2}\right)\[5pt]
\dfrac{1}{2}\sin x	&= \sin \left( \dfrac{x}{2}\right) \cos  \left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right).
  }
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\eqalign{
		\int \sin \left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) \cos \left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) \, \textrm{d}x&=\int \dfrac{1}{2}\sin {x} \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
								&=\dfrac{1}{2} \int \sin {x} \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
								&=\dfrac{1}{2} \left( - \cos {x}\right )+C \[5pt]
								&=-\dfrac{1}{2} \cos {x}+C.	
	}
$$

We can use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
\cos^2\theta -\sin^2\theta=\cos 2\theta.
$$

Letting $\theta = 3x$ gives

$$
\cos^2 3x - \sin^2 3x = \cos 6x,
$$

and therefore,

$$
\eqalign{
		{\int} \left(\cos^2 3x - \sin^2 3x\right ) \, \textrm{d}x&=\int  \cos 6x\, \textrm{d}x\
								&=\dfrac{1}{6}\sin6x+ C.\
                                                                
	}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the $\cos^2{x}$ term, given by

$$
\cos{2x} =2\cos^2 x -1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
\cos^2 x = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\cos 2x +1 \right).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\eqalign{
		\int \cos^2 x \, \textrm{d}x&=\int  \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\cos 2x +1 \right) \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
								&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int ( \cos {2x} +1) \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
                                                                 &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\sin {2x} +x\right) + C\[5pt]
								&= \dfrac{1}{4}\sin {2x} +\dfrac{1}{2}x + C.
								
	}
$$
